title: Persistent Pain
lead: Microbial products, immune activation and sensitised pain pathways.

steps.label: The gut observation
steps.heading: A microbiome difference in people with back pain
paragraphs: In the Sima study, 28 people with persistent low back pain were compared with 28 healthy people matched for age, sex and BMI. The pain group did not have advanced disc degeneration. Researchers sequenced bacterial 16S rRNA genes in stool to compare the microbial communities.

The pain group had lower within-sample microbial diversity. Prevotella was more abundant and Parabacteroides less abundant. These are measurements of community composition—not measurements of cytokines, intestinal permeability or pain-causing bacterial activity.
The next biological question is how an altered community could influence pain outside the intestine. The following stages trace the immune and neural mechanisms proposed in the lecture.
steps.note: Human observation · 28 cases + 28 controls. The causal route remains to be tested in this population.

steps.label: Microbial sensing
steps.heading: How microbial material becomes an immune signal
paragraphs: LPS is a component of the outer membrane of many Gram-negative bacteria. When it reaches responsive host cells, it can activate the TLR4 receptor system. This turns on transcription factors including NF-κB, increasing production of inflammatory mediators such as TNF, IL-6 and the IL-1β precursor.
IL-1β has another processing step. Inflammasomes can activate caspase-1, which cleaves its precursor into mature IL-1β. This separates making the raw protein from releasing an active signal.

The intestinal barrier controls contact between the microbial community and deeper tissues. The lecture proposes that increased passage of microbial material could sustain immune stimulation. The back-pain pilot did not measure that passage.
steps.note: Mechanistic route · microbial sensing is established biology; its contribution to this back-pain cohort was not measured.

steps.label: Pain sensitivity
steps.heading: Cytokines can change how pain pathways respond
paragraphs: Pain-sensing neurons convert potentially damaging stimuli into electrical signals. Inflammatory mediators can lower their activation threshold: a smaller stimulus can then produce a stronger response. That is one route from immune activation to increased pain sensitivity.

In spinal pain circuits, microglia and astrocytes interact with neurons. Experimental pain research examines how IL-1β, TNF and other mediators alter excitatory and inhibitory signalling within these circuits. Continued immune–neural interaction can help maintain sensitisation.
This explains why the lecture follows a gut–immune–nerve route. It does not require assuming that bacteria themselves travelled into a disc, or that every case of persistent pain began in the gut.
steps.note: Proposed connection in persistent back pain · stool sequencing alone does not demonstrate neural sensitisation by gut-derived signals.

steps.label: Immune restraint
steps.heading: IL-1Ra blocks a receptor; IL-10 changes cell behaviour
paragraphs: IL-1Ra binds the receptor used by IL-1α and IL-1β but does not assemble the activating signalling complex. It therefore blocks an entry point into the IL-1 response.

IL-10 works differently. It activates its own receptor on immune cells and changes their gene expression, reducing production of inflammatory mediators. One regulator competes at a receptor; the other tells responding cells to reduce inflammatory activity.

The lecture also follows butyrate from microbial fermentation into immune regulation, including the HCAR2 receptor. This is a mechanistic research direction. The back-pain study did not test butyrate, fasting, probiotics or a treatment targeting these pathways.
steps.note: Human feedback example · IL-6 infusion increased IL-1Ra and IL-10. Whether manipulating these routes improves gut-associated back pain is a separate experiment.

title: IBD
lead: Microbial sensing, intestinal tissue and a response that persists.

steps.label: The barrier
steps.heading: Intestinal tissue separates microbes from immune cells
paragraphs: The gut lining is a single layer of epithelial cells, supported by mucus, antimicrobial proteins and immune cells underneath. It allows nutrients to cross while controlling access of microbes and their products to deeper tissue.

Crohn’s disease can involve different parts of the digestive tract and deeper layers of its wall. Ulcerative colitis affects the colon and rectum, with inflammation centred on the mucosal lining. Both involve interacting changes in tissue, immunity and the microbial environment.

Inflammation changes that environment: oxygen availability, mucus, nutrient sources and transit can all shift. Microbial changes can therefore be both an influence on inflammation and a consequence of damaged tissue.
steps.note: IBD = inflammatory bowel disease. IBS is a different condition and does not mean the same tissue inflammation.

sources.title: NIDDK · inflammatory bowel disease

steps.label: The IL-23 circuit
steps.heading: Microbial sensing can sustain IL-17-producing cells
paragraphs: Dendritic cells and macrophages respond to microbial material and can produce IL-23. IL-23 acts on responsive lymphocytes, including Th17 cells and group 3 innate lymphoid cells.

These cells can produce IL-17 and IL-22. IL-17 acts on epithelial and stromal cells to increase antimicrobial responses and chemokines that recruit neutrophils. IL-22 acts directly on epithelial cells, supporting antimicrobial protein production and repair.
This creates a chain from microbial sensing to immune-cell behaviour to barrier function. IL-23 is important in experimental intestinal inflammation and is a target of IBD medicines.
steps.note: Experimental mechanism · IL-23 has been tested in models of innate and T-cell-mediated intestinal inflammation.

steps.label: Regulation
steps.heading: IL-10 restrains the cells that produce inflammation
paragraphs: Macrophages and dendritic cells help decide how strongly to respond to microbial material. IL-10 activates receptor-linked STAT3 signalling in these and other immune cells, limiting inflammatory mediator production.

Without effective regulation, repeated contact with the microbial environment can provoke sustained responses. IL-10-deficient mice develop chronic enterocolitis, making this an unusually clear experimental demonstration of lost immune restraint.

TNF provides a complementary clinical connection: suppressing TNF can improve disease in selected people with IBD. The treatment acts on a defined signalling pathway rather than removing all immune activity.
steps.note: Mouse experiment · removing IL-10 leads to intestinal disease. The human treatment example targets a different molecule, TNF.

steps.label: Defence & repair
steps.heading: IL-17 and IL-22 act at the barrier
paragraphs: IL-17 helps intestinal tissue recruit neutrophils and defend against extracellular bacteria and fungi. IL-22 helps epithelial cells produce antimicrobial proteins and regenerate damaged tissue through STAT3 signalling.

These functions explain why the next step cannot simply be “block every inflammatory cytokine.” In a randomised Crohn’s trial, the IL-17A-blocking medicine secukinumab was ineffective, with adverse outcomes raising concern.

The useful distinction is between the signal-producing immune cell, the receiving tissue cell and the response being changed. IL-23, IL-17 and IL-22 are connected, but blocking one is not biologically equivalent to blocking another.
steps.note: Human trial + mouse mechanism · IL-17A blockade and IL-22-dependent epithelial healing test different parts of this circuit.

title: Gut–Lung Axis
lead: How gut metabolites influence immune responses in the airways.

steps.label: Microbial metabolism
steps.heading: Fibre fermentation makes circulating immune inputs
paragraphs: Some dietary carbohydrates reach the colon, where microbes ferment them into short-chain fatty acids including acetate, propionate and butyrate. These molecules can act locally and some enter the circulation.
Short-chain fatty acids affect host cells through receptors and changes in gene regulation. Their influence can extend to immune-cell development and function outside the gut.
This is the starting point of a gut–lung mechanism: the intestine changes the chemical inputs reaching the immune system, which can change the response to a challenge in the lungs.
steps.note: Mouse experiments connect microbial fibre metabolism with allergic airway responses and influenza outcomes.

sources.title: Microbial fibre metabolism and allergic airway disease · mouse experiment

steps.label: Recruitment
steps.heading: Airway cells recruit specific kinds of white blood cell
paragraphs: Airway epithelial cells and resident immune cells sense infection or injury. Signals including IL-1 and TNF stimulate further cytokine and chemokine production in the tissue.

CXCL8 guides neutrophils towards a responding site. CCL2 helps recruit monocytes. These cells bring antimicrobial activity, but their enzymes, oxidants and inflammatory signals can also contribute to injury.

Gut-derived influences can change the cells available to participate and how strongly they respond. In mouse influenza experiments, dietary fibre altered myeloid-cell responses and reduced damaging neutrophil-associated inflammation.
steps.note: Species detail · mice use other neutrophil chemokines, including CXCL1; CXCL8 is shown here as a human recruitment signal.

steps.label: Antiviral defence
steps.heading: Interferons prepare cells to resist viruses
paragraphs: Cells detect viral nucleic acids and produce type I interferons, including IFN-α and IFN-β. These bind IFNAR receptors on infected and neighbouring cells.

Receptor signalling activates STAT proteins, which switch on interferon-stimulated genes. The resulting proteins interfere with viral replication and spread. This antiviral programme is distinct from bringing neutrophils into tissue.

The fibre–influenza mouse study also found changes in CD8 T-cell metabolism and antiviral responses. The gut can influence several branches of defence at once; it is not only a source of inflammatory material.
steps.note: Animal mechanism · the dietary experiment does not establish a fibre or probiotic treatment for human respiratory infection.

steps.label: Allergy & mucus
steps.heading: Epithelial alarms activate a different immune circuit
paragraphs: Damaged or stimulated barrier cells can release IL-33 and IL-25. These signals activate group 2 innate lymphoid cells, which can produce IL-5 and IL-13.
IL-5 supports eosinophils. IL-13 increases mucus-producing responses and alters tissue function. The same general programme contributes to intestinal worm expulsion and allergic airway inflammation.

The gut–lung axis therefore contains several routes: microbial metabolites, immune-cell development, antiviral responses and type 2 barrier signalling. Following a specific cell and receptor makes each route understandable.
